title: The Water Cycle
learningObjectives: Explain evaporation and its energy source
Connect the processes in a repeating cycle

segments.heading: A journey without an end
segments.body:
The water in a lake, a cloud, and a raindrop is part of one connected system. Water moves between Earth's surface and the atmosphere. It can change between liquid water, water vapor, and ice as it moves. We call this continuing movement the water cycle. There is no single starting point and no final step.

In this lesson, we will follow one possible journey: liquid water evaporates, water vapor condenses into droplets, water falls as precipitation, and it collects on or below the ground. Real water takes many different routes. Some stays in an ocean or underground for a long time. Some returns to the air much sooner.

The Sun supplies energy for evaporation. Gravity helps bring precipitation down and moves water downhill. Keep these two drivers in mind as you explore each part of the cycle.
segments.keyIdea: Water keeps moving. The cycle has no single beginning or end.
segments.diagramDescription: A lake below a cloud, with arrows connecting evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.

segments.heading: From water to water vapor
segments.body:
Imagine a shallow puddle after a rainy morning. Later, the Sun comes out. By afternoon the puddle is smaller, even though no water has flowed away. Some of the liquid water has changed into water vapor, a gas, and mixed with the air. This change is called evaporation.

Energy from the Sun warms water at Earth's surface. With enough energy, some water molecules leave the liquid surface and enter the air. Evaporation can happen from oceans, lakes, rivers, wet soil, and wet clothes. Water does not have to boil for evaporation to occur. Water vapor itself is invisible; the white shapes in clouds are not invisible water vapor.

Warmer conditions often speed up evaporation. Moving air can also carry water vapor away from a wet surface. These ideas help explain why washing may dry faster on a warm, breezy day.
segments.keyIdea: Evaporation changes liquid water into invisible water vapor.
segments.diagramDescription: An upward arrow from the lake shows liquid water entering the atmosphere as water vapor. The Sun provides energy.

segments.heading: Small droplets, big clouds
segments.body:
Water vapor in the air can change back into liquid water. This change is called condensation. When moist air cools sufficiently, some water vapor condenses into tiny droplets, often on small particles in the air. Many of these tiny droplets together can form a cloud. Clouds can also contain ice crystals.

You can notice condensation much closer to home. Think of a cold, sealed glass on a warm day. Water droplets may appear on its outside. These droplets do not pass through the glass. Water vapor in the surrounding air cools near the cold surface and changes into liquid droplets.

Evaporation and condensation are opposite changes between liquid water and water vapor. Cooling does not make new water appear from nothing. It changes the state of water already present. The droplets in a cloud are tiny enough to remain suspended in moving air until other processes help them grow.
segments.keyIdea: Condensation changes water vapor into liquid droplets.
segments.diagramDescription: A cloud of tiny water droplets represents water vapor that has cooled and condensed.

segments.heading: The journey back to Earth
segments.body:
Cloud droplets and ice particles can grow as they collide or collect more water. When particles are large enough to fall through the air to Earth's surface, water returns as precipitation. Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are forms of precipitation. Which form reaches the ground depends on conditions in the cloud and in the air below it.

Gravity pulls falling water downward. A cloud does not need to disappear completely when it rains, and not every cloud produces precipitation that reaches the ground. Some falling water evaporates along the way. The water cycle has more than one possible path.

After precipitation reaches the surface, its journey continues. Rain may land directly in an ocean or lake. Snow may remain frozen until it melts. Water reaching land may flow over the surface or soak into the soil. Next we will connect these routes to the rest of the cycle.
segments.keyIdea: Precipitation is water falling from clouds to the surface.
segments.diagramDescription: Downward rain lines from a cloud show precipitation falling toward the land and lake.

segments.heading: Back together. Around again.
segments.eyebrow: Every ending is a new beginning
segments.body:
After rain reaches the ground, some water flows downhill across the land. This surface flow is called runoff. It can enter streams and rivers, which carry water toward lakes and oceans. Some water soaks into the ground, a process called infiltration. Water below the ground may be stored or move slowly through spaces in soil and rock.

We can use collection to describe water gathering in places such as lakes and oceans. Collected water can later evaporate again. The same water can take different routes through the cycle, and each route may take a different amount of time. Our four-part diagram is a useful simplified model, not every possible pathway.

Now connect the ideas: energy helps liquid water evaporate; cooling can lead to condensation; precipitation brings water back down; and water collects or moves through the ground and surface. These connected processes repeat. Try explaining the journey from a lake to a cloud and back without looking at the diagram.
segments.keyIdea: Water collects, flows or soaks in, and can return to the air again.
segments.diagramDescription: Water flows down the hillside into the lake; the cycle connects back to evaporation.
